title: Data Structures
tagline: Asymptotic analysis, arrays and linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, trees, search trees, heaps and graph representations
summary: Data structures organise information so that the operations a program needs are fast. This course introduces asymptotic analysis and then the essential structures — dynamic arrays and linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, binary search trees and their balanced variants, heaps and priority queues, and graph representations — with their costs and the trade-offs between them.
overview: A **data structure** is a way of organising information in memory so that the operations a program needs — look up a key, add an item, find the smallest, list the neighbours of a vertex — are fast. Choosing the right one often matters more than any other decision in a program: the difference between a hash table and a list, or between a balanced tree and an unbalanced one, can be the difference between a millisecond and an hour. This course studies the essential structures that every programmer uses and every later course in computer science builds on.

It begins with the language of cost, **asymptotic analysis**, in which each operation is described by how its running time grows with the input — $O(1)$, $O(\log n)$, $\Theta(n)$ — in the worst case, on average under a stated assumption, or amortised over a sequence. It then builds up from the two basic ways of storing data, contiguous **arrays** and linked **nodes**: dynamic arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and deques; **hash tables**, which give expected constant-time lookup; **trees** and their traversals; **binary search trees** and the **balanced trees** (AVL, red–black, B-trees) that guarantee logarithmic height; **heaps** and priority queues; and finally the **representation of graphs**, on which the algorithms of the next course run.

Every structure is presented in the same way: the abstract interface it implements, a concrete representation, algorithms with proofs that they are correct, and an analysis of their cost — followed by small Python (and occasionally C) programs that you can run and modify. The hard part is not the code, which is short, but the reasoning: stating an invariant precisely, seeing why an amortised or expected bound holds and what it assumes, and recognising which structure fits a problem. Work through the traces by hand before running them, and do the exercises; most of them ask you to prove or implement something small.
outcomes: Analyse the worst-case, average-case and amortised cost of operations and express them with $O$, $\Omega$ and $\Theta$ notation.
Implement dynamic arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and deques, and prove the amortised constant cost of resizing by doubling.
Apply stacks and queues to problems such as bracket matching, expression evaluation and breadth-first search.
Design and analyse hash tables with separate chaining and open addressing, stating the hashing assumptions behind each expected-time bound.
Traverse trees in preorder, inorder, postorder and level order, and use traversals to process hierarchies and expression trees.
Implement binary search tree search, insertion and deletion, prove them correct, and explain how insertion order affects height.
Explain how AVL trees, red–black trees and B-trees maintain logarithmic height, and prove their height bounds.
Implement binary heaps and heapsort, and prove that a heap can be built in linear time.
Choose between adjacency matrices and adjacency lists for a given graph and algorithm, and derive the cost of basic graph operations in each.
Select an appropriate data structure for a problem by comparing the costs of the operations it requires.

chapters.title: Asymptotic analysis
chapters.summary: Counting operations, cost models, and big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta notation.

chapters.title: Arrays and linked lists
chapters.summary: Contiguous and linked storage, dynamic arrays with amortised doubling, and singly and doubly linked lists.

chapters.title: Stacks, queues and deques
chapters.summary: Abstract interfaces with array and linked implementations, and applications such as expression evaluation.

chapters.title: Hash tables
chapters.summary: Hash functions, separate chaining and open addressing, load factors and resizing.

chapters.title: Trees and traversals
chapters.summary: Rooted and binary trees, pre-, in- and post-order and level-order traversals, and representing hierarchies.

chapters.title: Binary search trees
chapters.summary: Search, insertion and deletion, and why unbalanced trees can degrade to linear time.

chapters.title: Balanced search trees
chapters.summary: AVL trees, red–black trees and B-trees, rotations and guarantees on height.

chapters.title: Heaps and priority queues
chapters.summary: Binary heaps, building a heap in linear time, priority-queue operations and heapsort.

chapters.title: Graph representations
chapters.summary: Graph terminology, adjacency lists and adjacency matrices, and the cost of basic graph operations.

history.title: Hashing and chaining at IBM
history.detail: Hans Peter Luhn's internal IBM memorandum proposed placing records in buckets by a computed address, with overflow chains; open addressing with linear probing followed at IBM in 1954.

history.title: Linked lists in IPL
history.detail: Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon introduced linked lists in the Information Processing Language for their Logic Theorist program.

history.title: Binary search trees
history.detail: Tree insertion and its average-case analysis were published independently by P. F. Windley and by A. D. Booth and A. J. T. Colin; Thomas Hibbard added deletion in 1962.

history.title: AVL trees
history.detail: Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis published the first self-balancing binary search tree, guaranteeing logarithmic height.

history.title: Heaps and heapsort
history.detail: J. W. J. Williams introduced the binary heap and heapsort, and Robert Floyd showed how to build a heap in linear time.

history.title: The Art of Computer Programming, volume 1
history.detail: Donald Knuth's Fundamental Algorithms set out information structures — lists, stacks, queues, trees — and the analysis of algorithms in the form textbooks still follow.

history.title: B-trees
history.detail: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight published B-trees in Acta Informatica, the structure behind database and file-system indexes; Bayer's symmetric binary B-trees of the same year became red–black trees in Guibas and Sedgewick's 1978 formulation.

history.title: Universal hashing
history.detail: J. Lawrence Carter and Mark Wegman showed that choosing the hash function at random from a universal family gives expected constant-time operations for every set of keys.

history.title: Amortised analysis
history.detail: Robert Tarjan's paper 'Amortized computational complexity' formalised the analysis of costs averaged over sequences of operations.

history.title: Skip lists
history.detail: William Pugh introduced skip lists, a randomised alternative to balanced trees with expected logarithmic search time.

references.title: Introduction to Algorithms
references.authors: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein
references.note: Fourth edition. The standard reference: rigorous chapters on hash tables, binary search trees, red–black trees, B-trees, heaps and amortised analysis, with the proofs this course cites.

references.title: Algorithms
references.note: Fourth edition. Clear implementations (in Java) of every structure in this course, with left-leaning red–black trees, many experiments and an accompanying website.

references.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Volumes 1 and 3
references.note: Third edition of volume 1 (Fundamental Algorithms, 1997) and second edition of volume 3 (Sorting and Searching, 1998). The deepest treatment of lists, trees, hashing and their exact analysis, including linear probing.

references.title: Data Structures and Network Algorithms
references.note: A short, dense monograph on heaps, search trees, union–find and their amortised analysis, connecting data structures to graph algorithms.

references.title: Algorithm Design
references.note: Excellent on graph representations, priority queues and how data structures serve algorithm design; a good bridge to the Algorithms course.

references.title: Open Data Structures
references.note: A free, openly licensed textbook (editions in Python, Java and C++) covering array-based lists, hashing, binary trees, heaps and B-trees with complete code and proofs.
